When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

I should have protected others and I failed

issues.explanation: The profile only includes Memory and Negative Appraisals, with the formulation showing a strong reciprocal link specifically between these two nodes. The memory items are dominated by trauma-recall qualities and guilt on recall, but 'Body as Enemy' and especially the globally externalized appraisal 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' shift toward current somatic threat/general danger beliefs that are not reflected in the memory content and are hard to reconcile with the otherwise memory-centred formulation. Given no active Threat or Trigger links, these appraisal items do not align well with the specified cognitive pattern.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: This appraisal is hard to reconcile with the provided cognitive formulation. The only active connections are between Negative Appraisals and Memory, suggesting appraisals should be closely tied to trauma recollection and meaning-making about the event. A generalized interpersonal-danger belief ('You can never know who will harm you') implies an active Threat focus, yet Threat is otherwise unrepresented and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The other appraisal items are self-blaming and memory-linked (weakness, inaction guilt), so this one pulls the profile toward a different formulation not supported elsewhere.

vignette: Luis Ramirez, a 55‑year‑old Navy officer of Mexican descent, had served at sea for more than 30 years before being stationed as a liaison officer in a small coastal town that had recently been caught in the crossfire of a regional conflict. He had moved there with his wife, Sofía, hoping the quieter life would let him step away from the constant demands of command. But the war’s roar was far louder than any ship’s engines. During a sudden artillery barrage, Luis was standing in the market square when a shell burst mere meters away, shattering a window and sending shards of glass into the crowd. He saw a young mother clutch her crying infant, a soldier wounded in the back, and a cluster of civilians running for cover. Luis’s mind raced: he could not intervene, could not stop the shell, could not protect anyone. In that instant he felt a hollow terror, a conviction that he was a coward, that he was failing the people he was meant to serve. The next morning, when he woke to the distant rumble of gunfire still echoing through the town’s streets, he found himself staring at the old photograph of the market that had been his home for a decade. Every image he tried to dismiss seemed to surge back, sharper, more vivid, as if the shell’s impact had carved the memory into his very bones. Because he believes he is weak and that he failed to protect others, Luis’s thoughts repeatedly pull the traumatic scene to the forefront. Each time he conjures the market’s chaos, the guilt swells, and the recollection feels all‑sensory: he can taste the metal of shattered glass, hear the soldier’s sob, see the mother’s face in the dim light. The memory’s intensity is magnified by the belief that he could have done more. This belief, in turn, keeps his mind looping back to the event, so the vividness never fades. The full sensory reliving becomes a compulsion; it is the most potent trigger that Luis can still encounter even at his own desk. The vividness of the memory reinforces his negative appraisals. Each time the scene flashes with such clarity—seeing the wounded, hearing the desperate cries, feeling his own helplessness—it deepens the conviction that he is a weak person, unfit for leadership, a failure to protect. The self‑deprecating narrative that he never forgives himself for not doing more to stop the bombardment grows louder. The cycle tightens: guilt fuels memory, memory feeds guilt, and the loop spirals into his everyday life. At the naval base, Luis has begun to avoid any assignment that requires close interaction with civilians. He refuses to serve on humanitarian aid missions, even when the base requests experienced officers. In meetings, he speaks in detached, clinical language, refusing to show empathy or enthusiasm. The avoidance has not gone unnoticed: his commanding officer notes that Luis seems disengaged, and Sofía grows increasingly anxious, fearing his withdrawal will strain their marriage. He has also stopped attending family gatherings; the mere idea of hearing children laugh triggers the market scene so strongly that he feels compelled to leave before it overtakes him. For weeks now, Luis has carried a sense of dread that each day might bring a new trigger, a new echo of the shell’s explosion. He is terrified of the possibility that his guilt and perceived weakness might never subside, that he will remain forever haunted, that he will never be able to protect those he loves. What gives him the faintest hope is the desire to reclaim his sense of agency, to feel, even briefly, that he can choose to move beyond the memory. The decision to seek help now is driven by a desperation to break the loop before it erodes his career, his marriage, and his sense of self. Luis hopes that therapy might offer a way to reframe the narrative, to lessen the grip of guilt, and to allow him to function without the constant, all‑sensory pull of the past.
